opus-5.5.text:
Sure. The easiest way to see it is to look at where the cost comes from in ordinary softmax attention. For each token you compute a query, a key, and a value. To produce the output for one position, you take that query and dot it with the keys of every previous token, push those scores through a softmax, and use the resulting weights to average the values. So every token interacts with every other token. With a sequence of length L, you end up computing an L-by-L matrix of scores, which means the compute grows quadratically in L. At inference time the cost shows up differently but just as painfully: you have to keep the whole KV cache around, and each new token has to attend over all of it, so memory and per-step cost keep growing as the context gets longer.

The key obstacle is the softmax. Because of that exponential and normalization, you can't separate the query from the keys. You really have to form each query-key score explicitly.

Linear attention basically says: what if we drop the softmax, or replace it with some feature map, so the similarity is just a plain dot product between the query and the key? Then the output at position t is the sum over previous positions of (q_t · k_i) times v_i. Because everything is linear now, you can use associativity and regroup it as q_t multiplied by the sum over i of k_i v_i transposed. That sum, the accumulation of key-value outer products, is just a d-by-d matrix. It doesn't depend on the sequence length at all.

So instead of comparing the query against every past key, you maintain this fixed-size matrix state. When a new token arrives you add its k v-transpose to the state, and you read out by multiplying the query with the state. Each step costs a constant amount, so the total cost over the sequence is linear in L, and at inference you don't need a growing KV cache, only a constant-size state. That's why people say linear attention is really an RNN in disguise: it's a recurrence with a matrix-valued hidden state.

In practice there's a nice duality here. For training you don't want a purely sequential recurrence, because that's slow on GPUs, but you also don't want the full quadratic form. So we use a chunkwise parallel form: within a chunk you compute attention in parallel, almost like a small quadratic attention, which uses tensor cores efficiently, and across chunks you pass the state recurrently. That gives you something that's linear in sequence length but still hardware-friendly. A lot of my work, like the flash-linear-attention library, is really about making that chunkwise algorithm fast.

The trade-off, of course, is that compressing the whole history into a fixed-size state means you lose information. Softmax attention can do precise retrieval over the whole context, and vanilla linear attention is much weaker at that. That's why much of the recent progress, things like adding data-dependent gating or the delta rule as in DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet, is about managing that state better: deciding what to forget and how to overwrite old associations, so the fixed memory gets used more intelligently.

r001.rationale: It says ordinary softmax attention forms an L-by-L matrix of query–key scores, so compute grows quadratically with L.

r002.rationale: It explains that dropping softmax makes the expression linear and allows regrouping into a fixed-size key–value state updated recurrently, like an RNN.

r003.rationale: It states that each new token updates and reads the fixed-size state at constant cost, yielding total cost linear in L.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The simplest way to see it is to look at where the cost actually comes from in standard attention. In softmax attention, for each query you compute a similarity score against every key in the sequence, pass those through a softmax, and then use the resulting weights to mix the values. So if your sequence has length n, you're building an n-by-n matrix of scores. That quadratic term is the whole problem. During training it means memory and compute grow with the square of the context length, and at inference time it means the KV cache keeps growing, because each new token has to look back at everything that came before.

The softmax is what forces that. It's a nonlinearity applied to the scores after you've already taken the dot product between query and key, so you can't reorder the computation. You have to materialize the scores, normalize them, then multiply by the values.

Linear attention basically removes the softmax, or replaces it with a kernel feature map applied separately to the queries and keys. Once you do that, the attention output is just a product of three matrices with no nonlinearity in between, and matrix multiplication is associative. So instead of computing query-times-key first, which gives you the n-by-n matrix, you can compute key-transpose-times-value first. That gives you a small d-by-d matrix, where d is the head dimension, and it doesn't depend on sequence length at all. Then each query just multiplies against that.

The really nice consequence is that this d-by-d matrix can be built incrementally. For causal attention, you walk through the tokens one at a time and keep a running sum of the outer products of key and value. That running sum is your state. Every new token updates it with a constant amount of work, and every query reads from it with a constant amount of work. So you get a recurrent form, which is why people say linear attention is secretly an RNN with a matrix-valued hidden state. Total cost is linear in n, and at inference you have a fixed-size state instead of a growing cache.

The trade-off, of course, is that you've compressed the entire history into a fixed d-by-d matrix, so you lose some of the exact recall that softmax attention gives you. A lot of the recent work, including the things I've been doing on gated linear attention and DeltaNet, is about making that state smarter, how you forget, how you update, so that you keep the linear cost but close the quality gap. And on the systems side, there's a middle path between the fully recurrent form and the fully parallel form, which is the chunkwise algorithm. You process the sequence in chunks, do dense matrix multiplies inside each chunk so you get good hardware utilization, and pass the compressed state between chunks. That's how you actually make linear attention fast on GPUs in practice, not just linear on paper.

r001.rationale: It says standard attention forms an n-by-n matrix of query–key scores, creating the quadratic cost.

r002.rationale: It explains that removing softmax (or using a feature map) makes the matrix products associative, enabling a running-state recurrence described as RNN-like.

r003.rationale: It states that each token updates the state and reads from it with constant work, yielding total cost linear in sequence length.

astra-6.text:
The key is the order of computation. In ordinary softmax attention, every query is compared with every key. For a sequence of length N, that gives you N squared pairwise scores, so the computation grows quadratically with sequence length.

Linear attention replaces that softmax operation with a similarity function that can be factored into features of the query and key. Then we can rearrange the calculation: first aggregate the keys and values into a fixed-size summary, and then let each query read from that summary. We never have to compute all N squared query-key interactions.

For causal attention, that summary can be updated incrementally as each token arrives. So, holding the feature dimensions fixed, the total work grows linearly with the number of tokens. The important caveat is that this generally changes or approximates the attention function—it isn’t simply a different multiplication order that makes ordinary softmax attention linear.

r001.rationale: It says each query is compared with every key, producing N-squared pairwise scores, which is equivalent to forming an L-by-L interaction matrix.

r002.rationale: It describes replacing softmax with a factored similarity function and updating a causal summary incrementally, but does not clearly state that removing softmax’s nonlinearity enables an RNN-like recurrence.

r003.rationale: It states that with feature dimensions fixed, total work grows linearly with token count, implying constant per-token cost with respect to sequence length.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is the order of computation. In ordinary softmax attention, you form a score for every pair of tokens, so for a sequence of length N, you have an N-by-N attention matrix. That gives you quadratic computation in the sequence length.

With linear attention, you replace the softmax similarity with a kernel that can be written as an inner product of feature maps. Then you can reassociate the computation: instead of computing all the query-key pairs first, you aggregate the keys and values into a fixed-size matrix, and each query reads from that matrix. You can compute the normalization in a similar way.

For causal attention, you maintain that aggregate as a running state, updating it with each new token. So, with the feature and head dimensions held fixed, the total computation grows linearly with the number of tokens. The important caveat is that this generally changes or approximates softmax attention; it’s not simply a faster way to compute exactly the same operation.

r001.rationale: It says ordinary softmax attention forms an N-by-N matrix of scores for token pairs, giving quadratic computation.

r002.rationale: It describes replacing softmax similarity with a kernel that permits algebraic reassociation, then maintaining and updating an aggregate running state token by token for causal attention.

r003.rationale: It states that with feature and head dimensions fixed, total computation grows linearly with token count, consistent with constant sequence-length cost per token.
